The property at issue is 49-53 South Moger Avenue, a .37-acre parcel of land improved with a 10,319+/- square foot one-story retail building, divided into 4 tenant spaces. Tenants include the Westchester Bank, Chopt, a hair salon, and a large (4,800+/- sq. ft.) space facing the rear parking lot, which was vacant for five years before being leased at a nominal rent for use as back office and storage space. The petitioner challenged the town and village assessments from 2020 through 2023, presenting an appraisal indicating values ranging from approximately $3,000,000 to $3,500,000. The actual assessments indicated values ranging from approximately $4,060,000 to $4,900,000. The settlement provides for values starting at $3,400,000 and increasing to $3,800,000. These values are based on an analysis of income and expenses for the subject based on the actual and comparable data, and an analysis of investment return rates for properties of the subject’s type. The indicated unit values are approximately $330 to $370 per square foot of building area, which are in line with valuations of comparably sized properties of this type. The values reflect the fact that retail market rents have declined in recent years. This settlement will result in refunds of approximately $34,744 from the village, $41,444 from the school district, and $8,105 from the county. In our opinion this is reasonable and favorable to a potential trial, given market conditions and the specifics of this property. Either Party may terminate this Agreement, with or without cause, upon the giving of ninety (90) days written notice to the other Party. Upon the giving of such notice and the expiration of ninety (90) days, this Agreement will be of no further force and effect. 2. Scheduling and Use of Property – The School District and Village each agree to allow the other to utilize buildings and grounds (“facilities”) for recreational programs and activities when not needed for School District or Village purposes, respectively, in accordance with schedules to be agreed upon by the Parties and will take priority over renter(s) if an event has been scheduled. The Village and School District will provide hour-to-hour usage between two parties at a minimum when using facilities for sports/programs/events. 3. Fee Schedule – The School District and Village agree to waive fees for the other’s use of its facilities, provided that each Party will be entitled to charge the other for custodial time incurred as a result of the use of the facilities on a Saturday or Sunday (if no custodians are scheduled for the time of any event). 4. Except as may be mutually agreed to by the School District and Village, respectively, each Party will provide all supplies and materials, and furnish and compensate all personnel necessary to conduct that Party’s programs and activities. 5. Rules and Regulations – The Village agrees to abide by the School District’s rules and regulations attached hereto as Exhibit “A” and labeled as “Facility Use Requirements & Applicant Agreement as well as the School District’s Policy on Public Use of School Facilities and the Code of Conduct provisions relating to Public Conduct on School Property. 6. Damage to Facilities – Each Party will be responsible for repairing or paying for the cost of repair for damage caused by that Party to the facilities of the other Party. Each Party will have the authority to postpone, cancel or terminate any event at its facilities if it is determined that the safety of the users or the conditions of the facilities will be compromised. 7. Indemnification – Each Party agrees to indemnify, defend, and hold the other Party harmless, including reasonable attorney’s fees, from and against any and all liability, loss, damages, claims, proceedings or actions for bodily injury (including death), and/or property damage arising out of or in connection with the negligent acts or omissions of the Party using the other Party’s facilities, except to the extent of the negligence or willful misconduct of the other Party. Each party, upon receiving notice of a claim, proceeding or action under this provision, will promptly notify the other Party in writing of any claim, proceeding or action received, but in no event later than ten (10) business of days of receipt by the Party. 8. Insurance – Each Party will provide the other Party with the proper insurance requirements as set forth in the respective policies and procedures relating to public use of facilities. Each Party will provide the other Party with a copy of the certificate of insurance evidencing such coverage. 9. Compliance with Law – Each Party agrees that its use of the other Party’s facilities will comply with all applicable federal, state and local laws, ordinances, policies, rules and regulations. 10. No Assignment – Neither Party may assign this Agreement without the prior written consent of the other Party, which may be withheld for any reason whatsoever or for no reason. 11. Notices – Any and all notices, demands or other communications required or desired to be given hereunder by either Party will be in writing and will be validly given or made to the other Party if personally served or if deposited in the United States Postal Service, certified or registered mail, postage prepaid, return receipt request, to the address set forth above, to the Superintendent of Schools for the School District and the Village Manager for the Village. Each Party may change its address for purposes of this paragraph by written notice given in the manner provided herein. 12. Approval – This Agreement is subject to the approval of the Board of Education of the Bedford Central School District and the Board of Trustees of the Village/Town of Mount Kisco. 17. Upon the passage of a motion to consider from the floor, and the same appearing proper and necessary. BE IT RESOLVED that the Town of North Elba Town Board hereby introduces proposed Local Law No. ___ of 2026 entitled “A Local Law to Override the Tax Levy Limit Established in General Municipal Law §3-c,” reading and provided as follows: “TOWN OF North Elba LOCAL LAW No. ___ OF 2026" Law A Local Law to Override the Tax Levy Limit Established in General Municipal §3-c. BE IT ENACTED, by the Town of North Elba Town Board as follows: Section 1. Legislative Intent. It is the intent of this local law to override the limit on the amount of real property taxes that may be levied by the Town of North Elba pursuant to General Municipal Law §3-c, and to allow the Town of North Elba to adopt a budget for the fiscal year 2026 that requires a real property tax levy in excess of “tax levy limit” as defined by General Municipal Law §3-c. Section 2. Authority. This local law is adopted pursuant to subdivision 5 of General Municipal Law §3-c, which expressly authorizes the Town Board to override the tax levy limit by the adoption of a local law approved by vote of sixty percent (60%) of the Town Board. Section 3. Tax Levy Limit Override - Budget Authorization. The Town Board of the Town of North Elba hereby overrides the tax levy limit for the Town of North Elba for 2027 and authorizes the Town of North Elba, after completing all required procedures for the adoption of a budget, to adopt a budget for 2027 that requires a tax levy that is greater than the tax levy limit calculated for 2027 pursuant to §3-c of the General Municipal Law. Section 4. Severability. If any clause, sentence, paragraph, subdivision, or part of this Local Law or the application thereof to any person, firm or corporation, or circumstance, shall be adjusted by any court of competent jurisdiction to be invalid or unconstitutional, such order or judgement shall not affect, impair, or invalidate the remainder thereof, but shall be confined in its operation to the clause, sentence, paragraph, subdivision, or part of this local law or in its application to the person, individual, form or corporation, or circumstance, directly involved in the controversy in which such judgement or order shall be rendered. Section 5. Effective Date This local law shall take effect immediately upon filing with the Secretary of State. BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that the Town Board of the Town of North Elba shall hold and conduct a public hearing on the foregoing proposed local law on the 10th day of November 2026, at 5:00 p.m. in the forenoon of that day, to hear any and all persons concerning the same; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that the Clerk of the Town of North Elba will publish a notice of such hearing in the designated Town newspaper at least five days prior to said hearing. In order to minimize the threat of such damages and to achieve the purposes and objectives hereinafter set forth, this local law is adopted. 1.2 STATEMENT OF PURPOSE It is the purpose of this local law to promote the public health, safety, and general welfare, and to minimize public and private losses due to flood conditions in specific areas by provisions designed to: 1.3 (1) regulate uses which are dangerous to health, safety and property due to water or erosion hazards, or which result in damaging increases in erosion or in flood heights or velocities; (2) require that uses vulnerable to floods, including facilities which serve such uses, be protected against flood damage at the time of initial construction; (3) control the alteration of natural floodplains, stream channels, and natural protective barriers which are involved in the accommodation of flood waters; (4) control filling, grading, dredging and other development which may increase erosion or flood damages; (5) regulate the construction of flood barriers which will unnaturally divert flood waters or which may increase flood hazards to other lands, and; (6) qualify and maintain for participation in the National Flood Insurance Program. OBJECTIVES The objectives of this local law are: (l) to protect human life and health; (2) to minimize expenditure of public money for costly flood control projects; (3) to minimize the need for rescue and relief efforts associated with flooding and generally undertaken at the expense of the general public; 1 (4) to minimize prolonged business interruptions; (5) to minimize damage to public facilities and utilities such as water and gas mains, electric, telephone, sewer lines, streets and bridges located in areas of special flood hazard; (6) to help maintain a stable tax base by providing for the sound use and development of areas of special flood hazard so as to minimize future flood blight areas; (7) to provide that developers are notified that property is in an area of special flood hazard; and, (8) to ensure that those who occupy the areas of special flood hazard assume responsibility for their actions. 2 SECTION 2.0 DEFINITIONS Unless specifically defined below, words or phrases used in this local law shall be interpreted so as to give them the meaning they have in common usage and to give this local law its most reasonable application. “Accessory Structure” is a structure used solely for parking (two-car detached garages or smaller) or limited storage, represent a minimal investment of not more than 10 percent of the value of the primary structure, and may not be used for human habitation. Such flooding is characterized by ponding or sheet flow. "Area of special flood hazard" is the land in the floodplain within a community subject to a one percent or greater chance of flooding in any given year. This area may be designated as Zone A, AE, AH, AO, A1-A30, AR, A99. It is also commonly referred to as the base floodplain or l00-year floodplain. For purposes of this Local Law, the term “special flood hazard area (SFHA)” is synonymous in meaning with the phrase “area of special flood hazard.” "Base flood" means the flood having a one percent chance of being equaled or exceeded in any given year. "Basement" means that portion of a building having its floor subgrade (below ground level) on all sides. "Building" see "Structure" "Cellar" has the same meaning as "Basement". "Crawl Space" means an enclosed area beneath the lowest elevated floor, eighteen inches or more in height, which is used to service the underside of the lowest elevated floor. The elevation of the floor of this enclosed area, which may be of soil, gravel, concrete or other material, must be equal to or above the lowest adjacent exterior grade. text: October 2026 - DRAFT 2 Heritage and Horizons acknowledgments Planning Consultant Team Salem Town Council Sue Clary, Supervisor Scott Eastman Howard Law Brenda Levey Thomas McMorris Committee Members Sue Clary Tom Clary Julie Collier Edward A. Donoghue Larry Haber with planning & grant support from Michael Hatzel Jon Ketchum Shane Nolan Bob Perry Jim Sheldon Noah Simon Kay Tomasi Beth Ulion Jared West Wyatt Wesner Funding This document was prepared with funding provided by the New York State Department of State Environmental Protection Fund. The Salem NY Plan Contents 01 Foundation Introduction 5 Salem at a Glance 9 02 Vision & Framework Vision & Goals 13 Future Land Use Map 19 03 Recommendations Small Business & Economic Development 23 Arts & Institutions 29 Housing 37 Infrastructure 41 Agriculture, Natural Resources, & Open Space 48 Recreation 52 04 Implementation Turning the Plan into Action 55 05 Appendices Appendix A: Review of Local & Regional Plans Appendix B: Community Profile Appendix C: Public Engagement Summaries • Community Survey Summary • Stakeholder Interview & Focus Group Summary • Public Workshop Summaries • Planning Committee Meeting Summaries Appendix D: Detailed Zoning Framework All appendices are provided as a combined online supplement available on the Town of Salem website. 3 4 Heritage and Horizons • 1.o Introduction 01 FOUNDATION • INTRODUCTION The Salem NY Plan • INTRODUCTION Introduction The Town of Salem Comprehensive Plan provides a roadmap for the next 10 to 20 years, guiding decisions about growth, reinvestment, public facilities, land use, and resource protection. Building on previous planning efforts and extensive community engagement, it establishes a shared vision and a set of goals, recommendations, and actions intended to help strengthen Salem while preserving the qualities residents value most. A Comprehensive Plan serves as the Town’s foundational policy document, guiding local decision-making and future actions by identifying community strengths, addressing challenges, and articulating residents’ collective vision for the future. More than simply a planning document, it provides a framework for managing growth and change in a manner that reflects community values and priorities. The Comprehensive Plan establishes the basis for future land use decisions, zoning updates, infrastructure investments, capital improvements, economic development initiatives, natural resource protection, and community development efforts. This plan embraces the key principles of effective comprehensive planning by taking a comprehensive approach to the many factors that influence community life; maintaining a long-range perspective while remaining flexible to changing conditions; focusing on broad policy direction rather than prescriptive regulations; recognizing the relationship between land use, infrastructure, economic vitality, environmental stewardship, and quality of life; and serving as the Town’s primary policy guide for future decision-making. Through this approach, the Salem Comprehensive Plan charts a path that honors the Town’s rich agricultural heritage, historic hamlets, scenic landscapes, and strong sense of community while preparing for future opportunities and challenges. 5 6 Heritage and Horizons Why Update the Comprehensive Plan? Salem’s previous Comprehensive Plan was adopted in 1997. Since then, the former Village of Salem was dissolved; the Town has completed major planning efforts for Main Street, pedestrian connections, and wastewater; and community needs related to housing, agriculture, infrastructure, climate resilience, recreation, and local services have continued to evolve. This update brings those efforts into a single policy framework and addresses priorities that have become more prominent since 1997, including housing choice and rehabilitation, hamlet reinvestment, agricultural viability, infrastructure capacity, flood resilience, and connections among Salem’s arts, cultural, and recreational assets. The Plan also reflects extensive input gathered through surveys, public workshops, stakeholder interviews, focus groups, and ongoing collaboration with the Comprehensive Plan Committee, ensuring that it represents the shared aspirations of Salem residents. The Community Planning Process Developing the Comprehensive Plan was a collaborative process involving residents, elected officials, farms, community organizations, businesses, and planning professionals.. The planning team paired analysis of existing conditions and previous planning documents with extensive public input collected through surveys, stakeholder interviews, focus groups, community workshops, and regular meetings with the Comprehensive Plan Committee. This combination of technical analysis and local experience was used to identify priorities, test ideas, and refine the recommendations in later chapters. Throughout the planning process, New York State’s Smart Growth Principles served as a guiding framework for evaluating existing conditions, engaging the public, developing the Vision and Goals, and preparing recommendations. This approach emphasizes directing investment toward existing community centers, protecting agricultural and natural resources, supporting housing and economic opportunity, strengthening infrastructure, and improving long-term community resilience. Comprehensive Plan Committee The Town of Salem established a Comprehensive Plan Committee to guide development of the Plan. The Committee included residents, local officials, business representatives, farmers, and other community members who provided guidance throughout the planning process. Committee members served as important liaisons between the planning team and the broader community by reviewing draft materials, identifying priorities, assisting with public engagement, and ensuring that recommendations reflected local values and community goals. Committee meetings were held every two to three months throughout the planning process, were publicized in the local media, on the project website, and e-mail announcements, and were open to the public to attend. Meeting summaries are included in Appendix C. Building on Previous Planning Efforts This Comprehensive Plan builds upon and synthesizes recommendations from previous Town, County, regional, and State planning efforts, including: • Salem Comprehensive Plan (1997) • Washington County Economic Development Strategic Plan (2007) • Salem Main Street Renaissance Plan (2017) • Washington County Agricultural and Farmland Protection Plan (2017) • Washington County Tourism Study (2017) • Washington County Housing Transitions: Needs Assessment and Supportive Housing Action Plan (2019) • Forward Together Economic Resiliency Plan (2021) • Salem Pedestrian Connections Plan (2022) • Rural Workforce Transportation Plan (2023) • Adirondack Gateway Safety Action Plan (2025) • Other applicable local laws, zoning updates, and planning initiatives completed since adoption of the previous Comprehensive Plan Together, these efforts provide an important foundation for this Comprehensive Plan while ensuring that recommendations remain coordinated with broader regional initiatives. The Salem NY Plan Planning Framework: Smart Growth Principles The Salem Comprehensive Plan was prepared with funding assistance from the New York State Department of State through the Environmental Protection Fund Smart Growth Comprehensive Planning Program. The planning process incorporated New York State’s Smart Growth Public Infrastructure Policy Act and Smart Growth Principles to guide development of the plan. Smart Growth is a planning approach that seeks to balance economic development, environmental stewardship, infrastructure investment, and community character while creating resilient communities that meet the needs of current and future generations. Rather than promoting growth for its own sake, Smart Growth encourages communities to build upon their existing assets, make efficient use of infrastructure, protect natural resources, and direct investment in ways that strengthen quality of life. For Salem, these principles reinforce many of the priorities identified by residents throughout this planning process, including preserving agricultural lands and scenic landscapes, supporting downtown revitalization, expanding housing opportunities, improving infrastructure, protecting natural resources, and maintaining the rural character that defines the community. New York State Smart Growth Principles This Comprehensive Plan was developed consistent with the following Smart Growth Principles established by New York State: 1. Allow for and encourage neighborhoods with a mix of uses, such as residential, commercial and community spaces. 2. Enable a diverse mix of housing types, providing opportunity and choice for people of all ages, abilities and incomes. 3. Prioritize infill and redevelopment of existing buildings to revitalize neighborhoods and downtowns, including areas around public transit. 4. Provide well-planned, equitable, and accessible public spaces for people of all ages and abilities. 5. Encourage compact neighborhood design and concentrated development around existing infrastructure. 6. Preserve open space, agricultural resources and natural resources. Land preservation directs development toward areas that are already developed, minimizing encroachment on open space and natural resources. 7. Prioritize transportation options that are safe and accessible for everyone, including pedestrians, cyclists and public transit users. 8. Promote climate resiliency and adaptation, preferably through nature-based solutions, and reduce greenhouse gas emissions. 9. Build on unique traits to create an attractive and welcoming community with a strong sense of place. Each community has unique attributes, such as historic buildings, natural surroundings, local traditions, or small businesses. 10. Engage in an inclusive, collaborative public planning process that considers the needs and character of the community. Throughout this Comprehensive Plan, these principles are reflected in the vision, goals, recommendations, and implementation strategy. Collectively, they provide a framework for guiding future land use decisions, infrastructure investments, economic development initiatives, environmental stewardship, and community improvements in a manner that is consistent with Salem’s values and long-term aspirations. 7 Heritage and Horizons 8 Public Participation Community engagement was central to development of the Salem Comprehensive Plan. The Town employed a variety of outreach methods designed to ensure that residents, businesses, property owners, farmers, seasonal residents, and other stakeholders had multiple opportunities to participate throughout the planning process. These efforts generated valuable feedback that helped shape the community vision, goals, and recommendations. Public participation activities included: • Community Survey: An online and printed survey collected community input regarding priorities, challenges, opportunities, and future goals across a range of planning topics. • Stakeholder Interviews and Focus Groups: Interviews and focus group discussions were conducted with Town officials, community organizations, businesses, agricultural representatives, emergency service providers, educators, and other stakeholders to better understand local issues and opportunities. • Community Workshops: Public workshops invited residents to discuss community strengths, challenges, future vision, and draft recommendations. • Public Hearings: Public hearings before the Comprehensive Plan Committee and Town Board provided formal opportunities for residents to review and comment on the draft Comprehensive Plan prior to adoption. These activities were promoted through the project website, social media, local media outlets, email announcements, flyers, and other community outreach efforts. Summaries of public engagement activities and comments received throughout the planning process are included in Appendix C. The Salem NY Plan • INTRODUCTION Salem at a Glance Salem is a rural community shaped by working farms, historic hamlets, waterways and open lands, a strong arts and cultural community, and a long tradition of civic involvement. Located in eastern Washington County along the Vermont border, the Town has maintained a relatively stable population. That stability has helped preserve Salem’s while landscape and settlement pattern, but it also means that an aging housing stock, limited infrastructure, changing demographics, and the need to sustain local institutions and businesses are especially important to the Town’s future. The Community Profile and public engagement process point to a consistent set strengths to build upon and emerging challenges that warrant proactive planning. Agriculture remains one of Salem’s defining assets and continues to shape both its economy and landscape. Nearly three-quarters of the Town lies within New York State Certified Agricultural Districts, approximately one-third of the Town’s land area is actively used for agriculture, and Salem contains roughly one-fifth of all farms in Washington County. Working farms, open fields, forests, and scenic rural vistas contribute not only to the local economy, but also to the community character residents consistently identified as one of Salem’s greatest strengths. Protecting farmland, supporting farm viability, and minimizing conflicts between agricultural and non-agricultural land uses emerged as recurring themes throughout the planning process. 9 10 Heritage and Horizons The Town’s development pattern reflects its agricultural heritage. Most new development has occurred as dispersed rural residential growth along existing roadways, while the former Village of Salem and the Hamlet of Shushan remain the community’s historic population and service centers. These compact areas contain a mix of housing, businesses, civic uses, and community facilities that distinguish them from the surrounding countryside and make them the most appropriate locations for future reinvestment and growth. Existing infrastructure, walkable street networks, and concentrations of services provide opportunities to accommodate additional housing, support small businesses, encourage adaptive reuse of existing buildings, and strengthen downtown vitality while limiting pressure for scattered development in agricultural and environmentally sensitive areas. Housing emerged as one of Salem’s most significant longterm planning issues. More than half of the Town’s housing was constructed before 1940, new residential construction has been limited, and available choices are dominated by detached single-family homes. Residents identified needs for smaller homes, senior housing, accessory dwelling units, quality rental options, and attainable housing for families and workers. At the same time, rehabilitation costs, property condition, and limited wastewater capacity can make it difficult to reuse older buildings or add housing in the Salem Hamlet. New tools, including the Washington County Land Bank, create additional opportunities to address vacant, deteriorated, and underutilized properties while expanding the range of housing choices. Salem’s population has remained relatively stable over the long term but declined modestly between 2010 and 2020. The Town also has an older population profile and a substantial number of households with limited financial flexibility. These conditions are closely tied to the future of Salem Washington Academy, local businesses, volunteer organizations, and community services: attracting and retaining families helps sustain school enrollment and the local workforce, while housing, transportation, health, and social-service options influence whether older residents can remain in the community. Salem’s proximity to employment centers in Washington County, the Capital Region, and Vermont creates opportunities, but many residents must travel outside the Town for work and services. The Salem NY Plan Natural resources are equally central to Salem’s future. The Battenkill, White Creek, Beaver Brook, other streams, forests, wetlands, floodplains, productive agricultural soils, and scenic landscapes provide ecological, recreational, and economic value while contributing to the Town’s identity and quality of life. Updated FEMA flood mapping and the Town’s history of flooding reinforce the need to consider floodplain function, drainage, stream corridors, and climate resilience in land use and infrastructure decisions. Protecting these systems can reduce risk while supporting agriculture, recreation, tourism, water quality, and public health. Salem’s arts and cultural institutions are unusually prominent for a community of its size. Salem Art Works, the Historic Salem Courthouse, the Georgi Museum, the Shushan Covered Bridge Museum, Bancroft Public Library, local artists, and community events contribute to local identity, tourism, education, and year-round community life. These institutions also create opportunities for stronger coordination, shared programming, placemaking, and creative-economy development. Public engagement repeatedly described the combination of agriculture, arts, history, and neighbors helping neighbors as one of Salem’s most distinctive strengths. Infrastructure is a recurring constraint, as well as an opportunity. The Salem Hamlet has public water but no municipal wastewater system, and previous engineering studies conducted by the Town documented how small lots, aging or undersized septic systems, and water-use restrictions can constrain restaurants, other businesses, building reuse, and new housing. Cellular service gaps, aging electrical infrastructure and limited three-phase capacity, sidewalk gaps, rural transportation needs, 11 and flood-prone roads also affect households, farms, businesses, and emergency services. Addressing these constraints in coordination with land use and development priorities is central to the recommendations that follow. Taken together, these conditions point toward a strategy of reinvesting in Salem’s existing hamlets and institutions while sustaining the working landscape around them. The Plan emphasizes practical improvements that expand housing and economic opportunity, support agriculture and community services, strengthen infrastructure and resilience, and preserve the rural character residents value. The vision, principles, and goals were developed through the community survey, stakeholder interviews, focus groups, and the first public workshop, then refined by the Committee. 14 Heritage and Horizons Vision A vision statement is the heart of a Comprehensive Plan. It expresses what Salem aspires to be, not just what it wants to do, but what kind of place it wants to remain and become over the next decade and beyond. This vision emerged directly from the voices of Salem residents, property owners, business owners, and community members who participated in surveys, public workshops, focus groups, and planning committee discussions throughout the planning process.
